title: Momentum and collisions
summary: Momentum, impulse, conservation, and elastic or inelastic collisions.
cards.0.p: Momentum is mass times velocity. It is given by p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. A slow truck is harder to stop than a fast ball, because its mass is large and so its momentum is large too.
cards.0.svg#9: the slow but heavy truck has a huge momentum
cards.0.key: Momentum is p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. Being fast does not by itself mean a large momentum.
cards.1.p: Momentum points the same way as the velocity. Choose one direction as + and count the opposite as −. Momenta add as vectors. Two objects with equal and opposite momenta have a total momentum of zero.
cards.1.svg#8: both are moving, yet the total momentum is zero
cards.1.key: Choose the + direction before you start a calculation. Velocity and momentum in the opposite direction get a minus sign.
cards.1.once.soru: Two 1 kg balls move toward each other at 3 m/s. What is the total momentum, in kg·m/s?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The momenta point in opposite directions. +3 and −3 add up to zero.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Opposite momenta do not add up, they cancel.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The two balls carry momenta of equal size in opposite directions.
cards.2.p: A net force acting for a time gives an impulse, I = F·Δt. The impulse equals the change in momentum (I = Δp). Its unit is N·s, which is the same as kg·m/s.
cards.2.key: Impulse is a vector too, and it points along the net force, which is the direction of Δp. If the force changes, use the average force.
cards.2.once.soru: A 50 N force acts on a ball at rest for 0.1 s. What is its momentum, in kg·m/s?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: I = F·Δt = 50·0.1 = 5 N·s, and the change in momentum equals this.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The force is multiplied by the time, not divided.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Force alone is not momentum. It has to be multiplied by the time.
cards.3.h: Area under the F–t graph = impulse
cards.3.p: If the force changes, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Area below the axis is impulse in the opposite direction, and it is subtracted. For a constant force the area is a rectangle equal to F·Δt.
cards.3.key: The area under a force–time graph gives the impulse, which is Δp. The area under a force–extension graph is work. Do not mix them up.
cards.3.once.soru: On an F–t graph the force rises steadily from 0 to 10 N over 4 s. What is the impulse, in N·s?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The area is a triangle, and ½ · 4 · 10 = 20 N·s.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: That would be right for a rectangle. But the force is not 10 N the whole time.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Impulse is the area, not the force. Take the time into account too.
cards.4.p: The Δp needed to stop is fixed. Since F = Δp / Δt, a longer time means a smaller force. That is why an airbag, helmet foam, and bending your knees protect you.
cards.4.key: An airbag does not reduce the impulse (Δp). It makes the time longer and so reduces the force.
cards.5.h: The momentum form of the second law
cards.5.p: The general form of the second law is Fnet = Δp / Δt. If the mass is constant, Δp = m·Δv, and this gives F = m·a. If the net force is zero, the momentum does not change.
cards.5.svg#3: if m is constant, Δp = m·Δv
cards.5.key: F = m·a is the form that F = Δp/Δt takes when the mass is constant.
cards.5.once.soru: If the net force on an object is zero, what happens to its momentum?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Since Fnet = Δp/Δt, if the force is zero then Δp is zero too.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: For it to decrease, there must be a net force opposing the motion.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The momentum of a moving object is conserved when there is no force.
cards.6.h: A ball bouncing off a wall
cards.6.p: When the direction changes, watch the sign. For a ball that hits a wall at speed v and bounces back at the same speed, Δp = m(−v) − m(v) = −2mv. If the ball stuck, Δp would be only mv.
cards.6.key: In a bounce the impulse is twice as large. A common mistake is to think Δp is zero for a ball that bounces back.
cards.7.p: If the external forces add up to zero, the total momentum of a system is conserved. The forces that colliding objects exert on each other are an action–reaction pair. These equal and opposite impulses cancel.
cards.7.svg#7: external forces add to 0 → total p constant
cards.7.key: The momentum one object gains, the other loses. Because a collision is brief, external forces such as friction are usually neglected.
cards.7.once.soru: Two skaters at rest on an ice rink push each other apart. What happens to their total momentum?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: There is no external force. So the total momentum, zero at the start, stays zero.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Both of them move, but their momenta point in opposite directions.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: The momentum was already zero at the start, and it is conserved.
cards.8.p: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Billiard balls come close to this. The swap of velocities you just saw happens only if the masses are equal.
cards.8.svg#10: p and KE conserved → equal masses swap velocities
cards.8.key: If a light ball hits a heavy ball at rest elastically, it bounces back. If a heavy ball hits a light one, both move forward.
cards.9.p: Most collisions are inelastic. Momentum is conserved, but part of the kinetic energy turns into heat, sound, and deformation. The total energy is still conserved.
cards.9.svg#13: with no external force, p is conserved in every collision
cards.9.key: Do not assume momentum decreased just because kinetic energy did. With no external force, momentum is still conserved.
cards.10.p: If objects collide and move together, the loss of kinetic energy is the largest possible. The common velocity comes from m1v1 + m2v2 = (m1 + m2)·v.
cards.10.svg#10: 12 J goes into heat, sound, and deformation
cards.10.key: The common velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass. Do not forget to add the masses.
cards.10.etk.soru: A moving object hits an object at rest and sticks to it. Change the masses and the speed.
cards.10.etk.girdiler.2.etiket: Mass of the object at rest
cards.11.p: If a system at rest breaks apart, the total momentum stays zero. The pieces fly apart with equal and opposite momenta. The recoil of a rifle and a rocket work this way.
cards.11.svg#4: before, everything is at rest: total p = 0
cards.11.svg#6: minus sign: the rifle recoils backward
cards.11.key: A rocket does not need air. In an explosion the kinetic energy increases, and this energy comes from the fuel or from a spring. Since KE = p²/2m, the lighter piece has the larger kinetic energy.
cards.12.h: Velocity of the center of mass
cards.12.p: The velocity of the center of mass is vCM = Σp / Σm. With no external force, vCM stays constant. When a firework explodes in the air, the center of mass of its pieces keeps following the old path.
cards.12.key: The center of mass is the average position that behaves as if all the mass were gathered at one point.
cards.12.svg#4: the CM stays on the path it would follow without the explosion
cards.12.once.soru: A firework flying through the air explodes. How does the center of mass of the pieces move?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.yazi: It continues on its old path
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The explosion is an internal event. It does not change the motion of the center of mass.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: An explosion does not destroy momentum.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The pieces scatter, but the center of mass follows the old path.
cards.13.p: In a collision in a plane, momentum is conserved in each component separately. If the incoming ball moves only in the x direction, then after the collision the y momenta of the two balls are equal and opposite.
cards.13.svg#13: no y momentum before → afterward the y parts are equal and opposite
cards.13.key: Add the momentum components, not the speeds. Write separate equations for x and y.
cards.13.once.soru: In billiards the cue ball comes in along x and hits a ball at rest. What is the total y momentum after the collision?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: There was no momentum in the y direction at the start. Each component is conserved separately.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.yazi: The same as the cue ball's
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: The momentum in the x direction is conserved, and the total in the y direction stays zero.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Without an external force, y momentum cannot appear.
cards.14.p:
• Momentum p = m·v is a vector, and its unit is kg·m/s.
• Impulse is I = F·Δt = Δp, and it equals the area under the force–time graph.
• For the same Δp, a longer time means a smaller force.
• With no external force, the total momentum is conserved.
• In an elastic collision KE is conserved too. In other collisions it decreases, and in an explosion it increases.
quiz.0.q: On a frictionless level track, a 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest and sticks to it. What is their common velocity, in m/s?
quiz.0.e: Momentum is conserved: 3·4 + 1·0 = (3 + 1)·v. This gives v = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s.
quiz.1.q: What happens to the total kinetic energy of the system in each event?
quiz.1.e: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved. For vehicles that stick together or get crushed, part of the kinetic energy turns into heat, sound, and deformation. In an explosion or a shot, pieces at rest start to move. The energy comes from the fuel, and the kinetic energy increases.
quiz.2.q: The net force on a 2 kg object at rest rises steadily from 0 to 50 N in 0.2 s, then falls steadily back to zero in the next 0.2 s. What is the object's final speed, in m/s?
quiz.2.e: The force–time graph is a triangle, and the impulse is ½ · 0.4 · 50 = 10 N·s. This equals Δp. So v = 10 / 2 = 5 m/s.
quiz.3.q: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall head-on at 6 m/s and bounces back at 4 m/s. The contact lasts 0.05 s. What is the average force, in N, that the wall exerts on the ball?
quiz.3.e: Taking the backward direction as −, Δp = 0.5·(−4) − 0.5·6 = −5 kg·m/s, with a magnitude of 5 N·s. The force is F = 5 / 0.05 = 100 N. Subtracting the speeds (6 − 4) is wrong, because the direction changed.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Match the momenta, bounce the ball, and crash the carts.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Momentum is mass × velocity. A 4000 kg truck moves at 5 m/s. Set the speed of the 1000 kg car so that their momenta are equal.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: 1000 · 20 = 4000 · 5 = 20 000 kg·m/s. If the mass is 4 times smaller, the speed must be 4 times larger. That is why a slow truck is hard to stop.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: A ball bouncing off a wall
A:adimlar.1.metin: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s. First let it stick, then let it bounce back. Play both cases and compare the change in momentum.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: When the ball bounces back at the same speed, what is the size of the change in momentum, in kg·m/s?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The speed is the same, but the direction reversed. Momentum is a vector.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That is the case where the ball sticks. When it bounces, the velocity goes from +10 to −10.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Δp = 0.2·(−10) − 0.2·10 = −4: the size is 4 kg·m/s, twice that of sticking. The wall gives the ball twice the impulse.
A:adimlar.2.metin: A 70 kg driver stops from 15 m/s, and Δp is always 1050 N·s. Make the stopping time longer and bring the force below 10 000 N.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The area under the graph, the impulse, is always 1050 N·s. As the time gets longer, the rectangle spreads out and its height, the force, gets smaller. At 150 ms the force is 1050 / 0.15 = 7000 N.
A:adimlar.3.metin: This collision is elastic. So kinetic energy is conserved along with momentum. The 1 kg cart A, moving at 4 m/s, will hit the 1 kg cart B at rest.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That happens when the carts stick together, and then kinetic energy decreases. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: A bounces back, B moves slowly
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That happens when a light object hits a heavy one. Here the masses are equal.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: A stops, B moves at 4 m/s
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Only this way are momentum (4 kg·m/s) and KE (8 J) both conserved. With equal masses, the velocities swap.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Now the carts stick together when they collide, so m1·v1 = (m1 + m2)·v. Choose the mass of B and press play. Make the common velocity 1 m/s.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: Since 1 · 4 = (1 + 3) · v, v = 1 m/s. The momentum was conserved at 4 kg·m/s and was simply spread over a 4 kg mass.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The 1 kg cart A, moving at 4 m/s, hits the 1 kg cart B at rest and sticks. Press play and watch the total kinetic energy at the bottom.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: With B at 1 kg, the kinetic energy dropped from 8 J to 4 J when they stuck. Which statement is true?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The total momentum is 4 kg·m/s both before and after. With no external force, momentum is conserved.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Energy is not destroyed, it changes form.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: 4 J went into heat and sound
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The common velocity is 2 m/s, and KE = ½ · 2 · 2² = 4 J. Momentum is conserved, and so is the total energy. Only the kinetic part decreased.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A 4 kg rifle will fire a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: At what speed does the rifle recoil?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It does not move at all
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The rifle pushes the bullet forward and gets an equal push backward (action–reaction).
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The bullet goes forward with a momentum of 0.01 · 400 = 4 kg·m/s, and the rifle recoils with 4 kg·m/s. The rifle's speed is 4 / 4 = 1 m/s. The kinetic energies are 800 J and 2 J, so most of the energy goes to the light bullet.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The momenta are equal, not the speeds. The rifle is 400 times heavier than the bullet.
A:kapanis.0: Momentum p = m·v is a vector, and its unit is kg·m/s.
A:kapanis.1: Impulse is I = F·Δt = Δp, and it equals the area under the force–time graph. For the same Δp, a longer time means a smaller force.
A:kapanis.2: For an object that bounces back, Δp is twice that of an object that sticks.
A:kapanis.3: With no external force, the total momentum is conserved in both collisions and explosions.
A:kapanis.4: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved. It decreases most when objects stick together, and it increases in an explosion.
